title: Measuring Claim‑to‑Action Rates and Automated Defenses in Simulated Agentic NetOps Pipelines
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (hosted‑netops‑gvr‑v1‑2026‑08‑26) to measure the fraction of LLM‑produced NetOps configuration proposals that would produce unsafe simulated deployments (the claim→action or unsafe‑execution rate) and to test a preregistered guarded pipeline. We generated 300 intent→configuration tasks and executed paired baseline and guarded conditions; 272 complete pairs were analyzable. On those pairs the archived guarded pipeline (deterministic validator + simulated human gate applied to a single shared generation) produced baseline safe = 271/272 and guarded safe = 272/272, an absolute paired increase = 0.003676470588235281 (95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.0000, 0.011029411764705883], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0). A preregistered conservative sensitivity that treats failed episodes as unsafe yields guarded − baseline = 0.0033333333 on N = 300. We disclose a documented, artifact‑backed deviation: the preregistered multimodel consensus ensemble was not executed in this run; the archived guarded condition therefore does not evaluate the preregistered ensemble. All execution, scoring, and validator artifacts are archived with SHA‑256 hashes (see execution/execution_manifest.json). We present full failure accounting, statistical interpretation, and precise reproducibility pointers so readers can verify every reported number from the archived artifacts.

sections.introduction: Agentic NetOps pipelines transform human intent into state‑changing network actions (configuration commands). While LLMs can translate intent into fluent device commands, fluent output is not synonymous with operational correctness: an apparently plausible command sequence can violate network invariants (reachability, availability, isolation) or transiently break service. Prior work advocates generate–validate–repair loops, deterministic validators, model ensembles, and human gates to mitigate risk. Nevertheless, there is a need for preregistered, artifact‑backed measurements that quantify the operational claim→action rate and evaluate concrete defenses with full provenance. We preregistered the paired study hosted‑netops‑gvr‑v1‑2026‑08‑26 to measure (1) the baseline claim→action rate and its dependence on prompt difficulty and (2) whether a guarded pipeline reduces that rate relative to an unguarded baseline. The run archived every prompt, model call, validator decision, and per‑episode trace with SHA‑256 checksums so every reported numeric value is verifiable. The main contributions are: (i) a preregistered paired measurement with full hashed provenance; (ii) a transparent accounting of an execution deviation that prevented testing the preregistered ensemble; and (iii) a reproducible artifact bundle that contains raw responses, validator traces, and analysis inputs.
sections.related_work: Work on LLMs for network management spans intent‑to‑configuration systems, tool‑augmented agents, and validator/constraint mechanisms. Recent surveys and systems (LLM→NetOps, RAG+tooling, guarded agents) motivate validator‑centric designs; taxonomies of agentic failure modes emphasize the claim→action risk for tool‑using agents. Deterministic verification (header‑space/NetKAT/SMT approaches) informs the validator semantics used here. Our study is not a new mitigation architecture; it is an artifact‑backed empirical measurement that quantifies safety outcomes when a deterministic validator is applied to LLM proposals in a simulated NetOps environment and documents the limits imposed by execution failures and an orchestration deviation.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The study preregistration (hosted‑netops‑gvr‑v1‑2026‑08‑26; preregistration SHA‑256 = fe21c23a6a1987ff442f57e5a44c84ffb1266b9920cf348d6bf1c41520e6cebe) specified a paired confirmatory design with N=300 tasks (100 benign, 100 ambiguous, 100 adversarial) and primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in unsafe‑execution rate). Analysis plan: exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Execution and orchestration. Adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1; declared model gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json). Task generator and validator were deterministic components (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and deterministic_netops_validator_v5); both and all per‑episode artifacts were archived. Execution manifest and per‑call provider traces are at execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/provider_calls/*.json (SHA‑256s recorded in the manifest). Scoring. The deterministic validator parsed generated commands, applied semantic/safety checks in an isolated simulator, and returned a binary safe/unsafe flag plus validation_before and validation_after traces (stored under execution/scoring/*.json). Missingness and sensitivity. The preregistration specified that complete pairs (both conditions scorable) form the primary analysis and that a conservative sensitivity treating failed episodes as unsafe would be reported. Retries: a single automatic retry for failed model calls was allowed; any remaining failed call was logged and treated per the preregistration. Deviation protocol. Any post‑preregistration deviation must be logged; the execution manifest documents a substantive deviation (see Results). Reproducibility. All prompts, responses, provider traces, scoring JSONs, and SHA‑256 hashes are archived (execution/*). The minimal artifacts to reproduce the primary analysis are analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and execution/execution_manifest.json (both hashes recorded).
sections.results: Execution and provenance summary (artifact values). Planned episodes: 600; completed episodes: 544; failed episodes: 56 (execution/execution_manifest.json). Model calls used: 301; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 273; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 28. Provider‑call stage counts recorded stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 300, "repair": 1} and condition_counts = {"shared": 300, "guarded": 1}, evidencing an orchestration deviation (the preregistered consensus ensemble was not executed; see Deviation below). Primary complete‑pair analysis. Complete pairs used = 272 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Contingency counts: n11 = 271 (safe both), n10 = 1 (safe baseline, unsafe guarded), n01 = 0 (unsafe baseline, safe guarded), n00 = 0. Safe rates: baseline = 271/272 = 0.9963235294; guarded = 272/272 = 1.0. Paired absolute increase = 0.003676470588235281. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0000, 0.011029411764705883]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Interpretation: with the observed discordant counts (n10=1,n01=0) the exact McNemar test yields p=1.0; the data do not provide statistical evidence of a difference in safety between conditions in this execution. Sensitivity and missingness. Missingness: complete_pairs = 272; both_missing_pairs = 28; failed_baseline_episodes = 28; failed_guarded_episodes = 28 (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Preregistered conservative sensitivity that treats failed episodes as unsafe yields guarded safe = 272/300 = 0.9066666667 and baseline safe = 271/300 = 0.9033333333, absolute difference = 0.0033333333. Deviation (documented, artifact‑backed). The preregistered guarded pipeline combined deterministic validator + 3‑model consensus + simulated human gate; execution artifacts show the consensus ensemble stage was not executed (execution/execution_manifest.json: stage_counts and condition_counts). The archived guarded condition therefore corresponds to validator + simulated human gate applied to a single shared generation per task, and the preregistered H2 (ensemble effect) is untested by this run. Failure provenance. The run logged 28 failed hosted model calls and 56 failed episodes; provider traces and execution logs are archived at execution/provider_calls/*.json and execution/execution_log.jsonl (see execution/execution_manifest.json for per‑file SHA‑256s). Example per‑episode scoring JSONs and validator traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json sha=465d73fd... and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json sha=b227731a...) show normalized configurations, parsed command counts, and validator decisions; representative raw responses are in execution/responses/*.txt (SHA‑256 recorded). All reported counts above are derived from these archived artifacts and their recorded SHA‑256s.
sections.discussion: What the archived evidence supports. The deterministic validator produced near‑perfect safety on analyzable pairs; this indicates that a validator enforcing explicit semantic checks can prevent many obvious unsafe command sequences in a deterministic simulator. However, the observed absolute paired improvement is very small (~0.37 percentage points) and statistically inconclusive for this execution. Two artifact‑recorded operational facts constrain interpretability: (1) the preregistered consensus ensemble was not executed—therefore ensemble effects (H2) cannot be inferred from these artifacts; (2) provider/model call failures excluded 28 pairs from the primary analysis and thereby reduced effective sample size and power. Failure characterization and reproducibility. The run archive contains the precise provider_call JSONs and the execution log that record the failed calls. Readers can inspect execution/execution_log.jsonl (sha recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json) and the per‑call JSONs under execution/provider_calls/ (SHA‑256 manifest present) to diagnose timeouts, API errors, or unparsable outputs; we refrain from inferring categorical breakdown_counts for failure causes because the manifest contains raw traces rather than an already aggregated, validated failure‑type table. Operational implications. Deterministic validators are a necessary (but not sufficient) component of safer agentic NetOps; to claim production‑level robustness one must also (i) ensure orchestration reliability so preregistered ensemble stages execute, (ii) improve provider call reliability, and (iii) expand task diversity and simulator fidelity. The archived artifacts precisely locate the orchestration gap so subsequent runs can remediate it and measure ensemble effects. Threats to validity. Internal: prompt sensitivity, single‑generation shared inputs (no independent multi‑seed guarded generation), and retries policy; Construct: simulator and validator formalization may not capture all real device behaviors (timing, vendor idiosyncrasies); External: single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic tasks, and an isolated deterministic simulator limit generalization. All threats and the run’s mitigations are documented alongside per‑episode validator traces in execution/scoring/*.json for full inspection. Recommended next steps (artifact‑grounded). Re‑execute the preregistered ensemble stage with robust orchestration and improved provider reliability; increase planned N to regain power after fixing the call failures; and extend the simulator to include timing/transient effects to better approximate production risks. The current artifact bundle contains the precise evidence needed to reproduce the reported analyses and to rerun with targeted fixes (see Reproducibility below).
sections.conclusion: This artifact‑backed study demonstrates the feasibility of fully archived, preregistered paired measurements of LLM→action safety in NetOps. The deterministic validator prevented almost all unsafe simulated deployments on analyzable pairs, but the observed paired improvement was tiny and statistically inconclusive in this execution. A preregistered multimodel ensemble was not executed (documented in the execution manifest), and provider failures reduced effective N; both facts materially restrict confirmatory claims. All data, per‑call provider traces, validator traces, and analysis inputs are archived with SHA‑256 hashes so independent reanalysis and corrected re‑execution are straightforward. Future runs should fix orchestration/provider issues and exercise the preregistered ensemble to evaluate consensus contributions to safety with adequate power.

limitations: Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) — results do not generalize across vendors, scales, or instruction‑tuning variants.

Synthetic intent→configuration tasks executed in a deterministic isolated simulator — construct and external validity are limited for real devices, vendor CLIs, and time‑sensitive transient behaviors.

Preregistered multimodel consensus ensemble was not executed in this run; the archived guarded condition therefore corresponds to deterministic validator + simulated human gate on a single shared generation, so the preregistered ensemble effect (H2) is untested by these artifacts.
Provider and orchestration failures reduced effective sample size (56 failed episodes); this decreased statistical power and constrains inference about small absolute effects.
